summary:
Samsun is a province on Turkey's Black Sea coast, and no province-specific rule, ban or enforcement programme governing transgender visitors is recorded there. What a trans visitor to Samsun faces is the national framework, which applies in the province as in every other.

That framework is contradictory on its face. Homosexuality has been decriminalised in Turkey since 1858 and sex-reassignment surgery has been legal since 1988, yet legal gender recognition still requires a court's permission under Article 40 of the Civil Code, with the applicant at least 18 years old, unmarried, and holding a medical report issued by a state-designated hospital. A visitor whose passport marker does not match their presentation is therefore dealing with a country in which recognised gender change is possible but slow, court-gated and medically conditioned.

The direction of travel is restrictive. A 66-page draft known as the 11th Judicial Package was leaked to Turkish media in mid-October 2025; it would amend the Turkish Penal Code, the Civil Code and six other laws. Human Rights Watch reported that the package would criminalise conduct deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' with terms of up to three years, and penalise participation in same-sex marriage or engagement ceremonies with up to four years.

For trans people specifically, the draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25, add mandatory infertility conditions and multi-stage evaluation hurdles, and expose providers to up to seven years' imprisonment and patients to up to three. Amnesty International's November 2025 factsheet concludes that the proposals would severely restrict, or make impossible, trans and gender-diverse people's access to gender-affirming healthcare, and would criminalise LGBTI+ people and those who advocate for their rights.

Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association have objected to the draft. Amnesty records it as the third set of proposed legal amendments targeting LGBTI+ rights in 2025, the earlier two having stalled in Parliament. The proposals are nationwide and would apply within Samsun as in every other province.
tangentialFactors:
The draft's trajectory matters as context even where its terms are not yet law: two earlier 2025 amendment packages targeting LGBTI+ rights stalled in Parliament before this one was leaked, so a measure's failure to pass has not reliably predicted its return.

Local authorities elsewhere in Turkey have acted against LGBT events on their own initiative. The Istanbul Pride parades of 2015 to 2018 were banned by local authorities after the 2013 and 2014 marches drew roughly 100,000 participants, which shows that provincial and municipal administrations in Turkey do at times impose restrictions beyond the national statute book. No comparable local ban is recorded for Samsun.

The Turkish military bars homosexuals from service and classifies homosexuality as a 'psychosexual' illness, an institutional position that sits alongside the civilian decriminalisation of 1858 and signals the depth of official pathologisation.
localsOnly:
Residents of Samsun seeking legal gender recognition must obtain a court's permission under Civil Code Article 40, be at least 18, be unmarried, and supply a medical report from a hospital designated by the state. Sex-reassignment surgery itself has been legal in Turkey since 1988.

Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence in Turkey since 1858, so the province's residents are not exposed to sodomy-style provisions; the exposure runs through morality-based offences, administrative restrictions and policing practice rather than through decriminalised conduct.

Gay men are barred from military service and their sexual orientation is recorded by the armed forces as a 'psychosexual' illness, a bar that affects resident men of conscription age rather than visitors.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the 11th Judicial Package has been introduced, amended or enacted after the mid-October 2025 leak is unresolved in the sources available here; the inventory records it as a leaked draft with two earlier packages having stalled, and does not confirm its subsequent status.

No incident, detention, arrest or complaint involving a trans visitor in Samsun is documented in the sources assembled for this record, so the province's practical enforcement pattern is not evidenced either way.

The current status of the Istanbul Pride bans imposed between 2015 and 2018, and whether any equivalent restriction is in force in Samsun, is not sourced here.

Whether the infertility condition and the age-25 floor in the draft would survive parliamentary negotiation, and how the Turkish Medical Association's objection was answered, remain unresolved.
